doc.title: Bobby Johnson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Hardest part of the road: Jim Crow and the 1952 change
summary: Hotels and restaurants were closed to them; he dates the change to about 1952 with mixed dances and the Civil Rights Act.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: When you were traveling on the road with Erskine Hawkins or any of the other bands, what was the hardest part of that, being on the road?

Well being on the road at that particular time, when I left Erskine the Civil Rights Act, this was before Martin and several other things happened. But the Civil Rights Act had just become a reality in our country. There wasn’t some of the things, some of the violence hadn’t started to happen. But people had begun to think for themselves you know what I mean. It even started down south. And there were hotels that we couldn’t go in, there were restaurants that we couldn’t eat in. And things, what were called during those days, that they were called Jim Crow in our society. But before Martin Luther King and President Johnson and other people saw things happening in our country, it changed overnight because if it hadn’t our country was doomed. You understand what I mean? You see what’s happening in other countries nowadays, they don’t even have a Civil Rights, and some of the — what baffles me about some of the countries, most of the countries are of the same color. But we had all kinds of different people of different races and everything that had to come together as one person. You know what I mean?

Yeah. Whether it was green, blue, yellow, white or whatever. But it had to be that way and this is not the end of it. You know? That’s just the way. Now this I can tell you about what year this started in. Around 1952. Now in 1952, dances started, mixed dances started. And people started speaking up for themselves for their rights. You understand what I mean? That’s just the way it was, it had to be that way you know? All right?
